name: Euclidean distance
seoDesc: Euclidean distance: a free math calculator that walks you through 63 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary: The Euclidean distance calculator is a free, no-sign-up math tool. Fill in the 20 fields it asks for and it works out distance straight away, with the formula shown underneath. It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Euclidean distance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Euclidean distance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports distance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the dimensions, the type (Dimensions and problem type) and the type (Dimensions and problem type)); then you type in the m (Second line [y = mx + c₂]), the distance (Result), the distance (Result) and the distance 2-3.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Euclidean distance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

X₂=X₁ + the square root of ((distance ^ 2) − ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₁ − K₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₁ − Y₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₁ − Z₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
Distance=the absolute value of (C + M × X₁ − Y₁) ÷ the square root of ((M ^ 2) + 1)
X₂=X₃ + the square root of ((distance 2-3 ^ 2) − ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₂ − K₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₂ − Y₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₂ − Z₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
X₃=X₁ + the square root of ((distance 1-3 ^ 2) − ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₁ − K₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₁ − Y₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₁ − Z₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
X₂=X₁ + the square root of ((distance 1-2 ^ 2) − ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₁ − K₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₁ − Y₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₁ − Z₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
M=the square root of (-1 + (the absolute value of (C₁ − C₂), 2) ÷ (distance ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Euclidean distance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Euclidean distance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Euclidean distance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 20 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Square y = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Euclidean distance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
